title: 1 Chronicles 4:11–23
context: The Judah lists continue with smaller clans and their settlements: the men of Recah, the line of Kenaz including Othniel (compare Judges 3:9), the descendants of Caleb the son of Jephunneh (compare Numbers 13:6), and several households of craftsmen, linen workers, and potters. Some ancient Greek and Latin witnesses add “and Meonothai” after the sons of Othniel in 4:13, which would make Meonothai a son of Othniel and explain his appearance at the start of 4:14; the WEB text here does not include those words. Mered’s marriage to Bithiah, a daughter of Pharaoh (4:18), is mentioned without explanation, and her identity is not known beyond this verse. The passage closes by noting that these records are ancient (4:22). Arminian and Reformed readers treat the section as shared ground: God preserved the families, trades, and towns of Judah, and the Chronicler honors ordinary work and obscure households as part of the people of God.

verses.text: Chelub the brother of Shuhah became the father of Mehir, who was the father of Eshton.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Chelub, Mehir, and Eshton begin a new set of names whose link to the earlier lines is not fully explained. The Chronicler preserves the records he has, and the verse reminds readers that the people of Judah included many branches whose stories were known to their own families even when they left little mark elsewhere.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly decline to force a connection the text does not state, and they see the verse as part of the Chronicler’s patient record of Judah’s households. Both traditions agree that the restored community could find its place in these lists, and that God’s care for his people included families whose names alone survive.

verses.text: Eshton became the father of Beth Rapha, Paseah, and Tehinnah the father of Ir Nahash. These are the men of Recah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that several names here look like place names, such as Ir Nahash, so that persons and settlements blend in the record. The men of Recah are remembered as a group, showing how family identity and home town were bound together in Israel and how both were treated as part of the inheritance God gave.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also note that founders and towns are intertwined in this verse and that the location of Recah is uncertain. Both traditions read the verse as testimony that God’s gift of the land reached down to particular towns and clans, and that the Chronicler wished the returning community to see those places as part of its covenant heritage.

verses.text: The sons of Kenaz: Othniel and Seraiah. The sons of Othniel: Hathath.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers recognize Othniel, whom Judges presents as the first judge raised up when Israel cried to the LORD (Judges 3:9). His appearance in a genealogy recalls a time of deliverance and invites readers to remember that God answered his people when they turned to him, a theme the Chronicler returns to often.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise connect Othniel with the deliverance recorded in Judges and see his name as a reminder of God’s faithfulness in raising up leaders. Both traditions agree that the brief entry places a known deliverer within the ordinary flow of Judah’s families, showing that God’s saving acts arise within the life of his covenant people.

verses.text: Meonothai became the father of Ophrah: and Seraiah became the father of Joab the father of Ge Harashim, for they were craftsmen.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Joab’s descendants are identified as craftsmen, with a place named for them. The Chronicler values skilled work as part of the life God gave his people in the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the reference to craftsmen as an honoring of ordinary vocation. Both traditions read the verse as evidence that God’s people included artisans whose labor contributed to the shared life of Judah.

verses.text: The sons of Caleb the son of Jephunneh: Iru, Elah, and Naam. The son of Elah: Kenaz.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers recognize Caleb the son of Jephunneh, remembered in Numbers and Joshua for following the LORD fully when others drew back (compare Numbers 13:6; 14:24). His descendants listed here carry forward the memory of a man whose faithfulness was rewarded with an inheritance in the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise recall Caleb’s faithfulness and the inheritance God granted him, and they see the listing of his sons as a sign of God’s continuing kindness to his household. Both traditions note that chapter 2 also lists a Caleb son of Hezron (2:18), and that the Chronicler records both lines without explaining how they relate.

verses.text: The sons of Jehallelel: Ziph, Ziphah, Tiria, and Asarel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the sons of Jehallelel include Ziph, a name also known as a place in Judah, though the relation between person and place here is not spelled out. The verse adds another household to the record and reflects the Chronicler’s desire to leave no family of Judah outside the remembered people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly treat the overlap of personal and place names with caution and do not press the connection. Both traditions see in the verse a quiet affirmation that God preserved even the smaller clans of Judah, and that the Chronicler’s audience could trace their belonging through such names to the people God had chosen.

verses.text: The sons of Ezrah: Jether, Mered, Epher, and Jalon; and Mered’s wife bore Miriam, Shammai, and Ishbah the father of Eshtemoa.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that the sons of Ezrah and the children of Mered are given in a compressed form that is hard to follow, and the verse appears to anticipate details in the next verse. The Chronicler is preserving family memory as it came to him, and the mention of Miriam, a daughter, again shows women within the record.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also note the difficulty of the verse’s arrangement and resist reconstructing it beyond what the text supports. Both traditions agree that the point is the preservation of Mered’s household and its link to towns such as Eshtemoa, and that God’s faithfulness to Judah reached into these intertwined families.

verses.text: His wife the Jewess bore Jered the father of Gedor, Heber the father of Soco, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah. These are the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered took.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the verse appears to describe two wives of Mered: one called the Jewess, and Bithiah, a daughter of Pharaoh. The text does not explain how this marriage came about, and her identity is not known from other sources. Her inclusion suggests that people from outside Israel could be woven into Judah’s families, a theme that fits God’s purpose to bless the nations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise refrain from speculating about Bithiah beyond what the verse says, while noting that a woman of Egyptian royal background is counted within the household of Judah. Both traditions see here a small sign that the covenant people were never sealed off from outsiders who joined them, and that God’s grace could embrace those from other nations.

verses.text: The sons of the wife of Hodiah, the sister of Naham, were the fathers of Keilah the Garmite and Eshtemoa the Maacathite.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that the verse speaks of the sons of the wife of Hodiah as founders of Keilah and Eshtemoa, with descriptive names such as the Garmite and the Maacathite. The details are obscure, but the verse shows how towns of Judah traced their origins to particular households within God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also note the obscurity of these relationships and the uncertainty of the descriptive titles. Both traditions agree that the Chronicler’s purpose is to link settlements and families, giving the restored community a sense that the towns of their land had long histories within the covenant God had made with Israel.

verses.text: The sons of Shimon: Amnon, Rinnah, Ben Hanan, and Tilon. The sons of Ishi: Zoheth, and Ben Zoheth.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the sons of Shimon and of Ishi are listed with no further information. Even these brief entries testify that each household mattered enough to be remembered as part of the people God had brought into the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the verse as one more witness to the Chronicler’s careful record of Judah’s families. Both traditions agree that the lack of narrative does not make the names insignificant, since the genealogies as a whole proclaim that God preserved his people through every generation, including those otherwise forgotten.

verses.text: The sons of Shelah the son of Judah: Er the father of Lecah, Laadah the father of Mareshah, and the families of the house of those who worked fine linen, of the house of Ashbea;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers recognize Shelah as the son of Judah through whom the third line of the tribe descends (compare Genesis 38; 46:12). The verse mentions a guild of fine linen workers, showing that the Chronicler remembered Judah not only by its rulers but also by its trades and the skilled labor of its families.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the significance of Shelah’s line, which survived when his older brothers did not, and they see God’s preserving hand in its continuation. Both traditions value the mention of the linen workers of the house of Ashbea as an honoring of ordinary vocation within the covenant community.

verses.text: and Jokim, and the men of Cozeba, and Joash, and Saraph, who had dominion in Moab, and Jashubilehem. These records are ancient.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that some of Shelah’s descendants are said to have had dominion in Moab, a detail the text leaves unexplained, and that the Chronicler adds that these records are ancient. The remark shows awareness that he is drawing on old sources and passing on what has been preserved rather than inventing it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also note the reference to Moab and the remark about ancient records, taking it as a sign of the Chronicler’s care for his sources. Both traditions agree that the verse should not be pressed for historical details it does not supply, and both see in it the long reach of Judah’s history under God’s providence.

verses.text: These were the potters, and the inhabitants of Netaim and Gederah; they lived there with the king for his work.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the potters and the inhabitants of Netaim and Gederah lived there with the king for his work. The king is not named, and the arrangement is not described further. The verse honors ordinary laborers and shows that service in the king’s work was part of Judah’s life within the land God had given.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise leave the king unidentified and see in the verse a respect for humble trades within the covenant community. Both traditions can affirm that the Chronicler includes potters alongside founders and warriors, a reminder that God’s people are made up of many callings, each with its place in the common life.
